title: The Dead God's Dream
subtitle: Within the bones of divinity, something still remembers how to dream

setting.name: The Dead God's Cradle
setting.description: Deep in the Astral Sea, far from any charted color pool or githyanki trade route, the petrified corpse of Auldrath tumbles in slow, majestic rotation through the silver void. Auldrath was the god of boundaries and thresholds — the divine custodian of the lines between things. Between life and death, between one plane and another, between what is and what could be. When the gods divided the primordial chaos into distinct planes of existence, it was Auldrath who drew the borders and held them firm. For this service, Auldrath was rewarded with a portfolio of immense power and crushing loneliness — the god of boundaries must stand at every border and belong to none. Auldrath died during the Dawn War, struck down by a primordial entity whose name has been scoured from every record. The killing blow split the god from crown to sternum, and the divine corpse fell into the Astral Sea, where it has drifted for eons beyond counting. Time does not pass in the Astral, and so Auldrath's body has not decayed — it has calcified. Divine flesh has hardened into a substance somewhere between stone and metal, shot through with veins of crystallized ichor that glow with a faint, pulsing amber light. The corpse is continent-sized: from the crown of the skull to the soles of the feet stretches a distance of roughly forty miles, and the outstretched arms span nearly thirty. Mountains of divine bone jut from the surface like tectonic ridges. Valleys of petrified muscle tissue form canyons hundreds of feet deep. The great wound that killed Auldrath — the split from skull to sternum — has become a canyon miles wide, its walls still faintly luminous with the residual energy of the blow that ended a god. Entire ecosystems have taken root in and on the corpse. Creatures that feed on residual divine energy — parasites of godflesh — have colonized every surface, from the microscopic organisms that form a thin, bioluminescent crust on the skin to the massive predators that nest in the eye sockets and hunt through the marrow caverns. These are not natural creatures; they are things that evolved in the presence of dead divinity, and they are profoundly alien. Some resemble insects scaled to nightmarish proportions. Others are geometric — crystalline entities that move by refracting light through their bodies. Still others are organic but wrong, as if designed by an intelligence that understood the concept of life but not its aesthetics. And beneath all of it, permeating every chamber and tunnel and surface of the corpse, is the Dream. Auldrath is dead. But Auldrath was the god of thresholds, and the threshold between life and death was part of the divine portfolio. In death, Auldrath stands at that threshold still — not alive, not truly dead, but dreaming on the border between. The dreams are not coherent. They are fragments: memories of drawing the first boundaries between planes, arguments with other gods whose names are forgotten, the terrible loneliness of standing at every doorway and belonging in no room. These dream-fragments manifest physically inside the corpse. Corridors rearrange themselves. Gravity shifts without warning. Characters may turn a corner and find themselves in a crystallized memory of a divine council chamber, or a nightmare vision of the primordial chaos that existed before boundaries, or a hauntingly peaceful meadow that Auldrath once dreamed of visiting but never did. The deeper you go into the corpse, the more powerful the dreams become, until in the skull itself — where a Confluence fragment pulses like a tumor in the dead god's brain — the boundary between dream and reality dissolves entirely, and the dreamer begins to dream of you.
setting.atmosphere: The first thing you notice is the silence. Not the silence of an empty room but the silence of a held breath — the silence of something vast and unconscious whose stillness is the only thing preventing catastrophe. The second thing you notice is the light. It comes from within the corpse itself: a deep amber glow that pulses through veins of crystallized divine ichor in a rhythm that is unmistakably organic. Not a heartbeat — slower than that. A breath-rhythm. The dead god breathes in light, and the entire corpse illuminates for three seconds, and then it exhales, and the light dims for five, and the cycle repeats with the patience of geology. Your eyes adjust to this rhythm involuntarily, and you find yourself breathing in sync with it, and that is when you realize that the corpse is not merely a place — it is a presence. You are inside something that was once aware, that may still be aware in some diminished and terrible way, and every step you take echoes through chambers that were once filled with divine thought. The air inside the corpse smells of ozone and ancient stone and something else — something sweet and faintly corrupt, like flowers left too long in still water. It is the smell of divinity decomposing, not into rot but into raw magic, and breathing it produces a faint euphoria that must be actively resisted. Sounds behave strangely: footsteps echo in directions that don't correspond to the architecture, and occasionally you hear things that cannot be there — the murmur of a vast crowd, the tolling of a bell made of light, a voice speaking in a language that you almost understand, that tugs at the edges of comprehension like a word on the tip of your tongue. The temperature varies wildly between chambers. Some are blood-warm, heated by residual divine energy. Others are cold beyond natural explanation, as if the absence of divinity has created pockets of metaphysical void that drain heat the way black holes drain light. And everywhere, at the edge of perception, you catch glimpses of things that are not quite there: a doorway that exists for a moment and then doesn't, a figure standing in the distance that vanishes when you focus on it, your own reflection in the crystallized walls doing something slightly different from what you are doing. The dead god dreams, and inside the dream, you are not entirely real — and neither is anything else.

keyLocations.name: The Approach
keyLocations.description: The corpse of Auldrath is visible from hundreds of miles away in the Astral Sea — a dark mass against the silver void that resolves, as you draw closer, into something that stops rational thought in its tracks. It is a body. A humanoid body of impossible scale, curled slightly as if in sleep, rotating with glacial slowness through the emptiness. The features are still recognizable despite millennia of calcification: a face of austere, androgynous beauty, eyes closed, expression peaceful, hands folded across a chest that has been split open by a wound that looks fresh despite being older than most civilizations. The skin has the color and texture of dark granite, but it is threaded with veins of amber crystal that pulse with that slow, rhythmic glow. As you approach, the silver compass given by Zerith-Ka begins to vibrate, its needle locked on the corpse's skull with unwavering intensity, and you feel a pull — not physical but psychic, a gentle tug at the edges of your consciousness, as if something inside the corpse has noticed you and is curious. The Approach is the region of Astral space within ten miles of the corpse, and it is not empty. A thin haze of residual divine energy creates a faint golden mist that thickens as you draw closer, and within this mist, things move. Divine parasites — creatures that feed on the ambient energy leaking from the corpse — drift through the haze in vast schools, ranging from thumb-sized luminous motes to predators the size of warhorses. Most ignore creatures of mortal origin, having evolved to consume divine energy rather than flesh, but some have developed a taste for the psychic energy of thinking beings, and they are drawn to the party like moths to flame. The surface of the corpse itself is a landscape of petrified flesh: vast plains of stone-hard skin broken by ridges of calcified muscle, craters where divine blood pooled and crystallized into lakes of amber glass, and the jagged peaks of exposed bone where the flesh has eroded away. Navigating the surface requires climbing, jumping, and occasionally rappelling across terrain that was never meant to be walked on. And everywhere, that slow pulse of amber light, breathing in and out, in and out, a rhythm that becomes as constant and inescapable as your own heartbeat.
features: Divine Haze (golden mist within 10 miles of the corpse) — the mist is residual divine energy made visible; breathing it requires a DC 11 Constitution save every hour or the character experiences mild euphoria and disadvantage on Wisdom checks for 1 hour; a successful DC 14 Arcana check allows a character to filter the energy and gain 1d8 temporary hit points instead; the mist provides dim light and light obscurement throughout the Approach

Corpse Surface Terrain — the petrified skin is rough and climbable (DC 10 Athletics) but unpredictable; every 500 feet of surface travel, roll 1d6: on a 1, a section of calcified flesh crumbles underfoot (DC 13 Dexterity save or fall 2d6 feet into a subcutaneous cavity); on a 2-3, a vein of crystallized ichor creates a slippery ridge (DC 12 Acrobatics to cross at full speed); on a 4-6, the terrain is stable

Amber Crystal Lakes — pooled and crystallized divine blood, some spanning hundreds of feet; the crystal is translucent and 2-6 inches thick; DC 15 Perception to notice a lake before stepping on it; the crystal supports up to 200 lbs before cracking; characters who fall through plunge into liquid divine energy (2d8 radiant damage per round, DC 15 Constitution save or gain one random minor divine blessing: darkvision 60 ft, resistance to one damage type for 24 hours, or ability to speak Celestial for 24 hours)

Psychic Pull — within 5 miles of the corpse, all characters feel a gentle psychic tug toward the skull; DC 10 Wisdom save to resist; failure means the character unconsciously drifts or walks toward the skull unless actively choosing a different direction; the pull intensifies to DC 13 within 1 mile, and DC 16 within the skull itself

Scale Reference Points — the corpse's features provide navigation landmarks: the Closed Eyes (each eye socket is 200 feet across and occupied by nesting parasites), the Folded Hands (the interlocked fingers create a maze of canyons), the Great Wound (the killing blow's canyon, miles wide, glowing faintly with residual primordial energy), and the Hair (petrified strands the size of ancient trees, forming a forest on the scalp)
encounters: A school of Luminous Motes (12 divine parasites, use will-o'-wisp stats with radiant damage instead of lightning) — they swarm toward the party's psychic emanations as the group enters the divine haze; they are not hostile but will attempt to feed on psychic energy, dealing 1d6 psychic damage per round to any creature they surround; a DC 14 Arcana check reveals they can be dispersed by channeling divine or radiant energy outward, or simply outflown

A Void Grazer (use bulette stats, CR 5, but replace burrowing with flying 40 ft and all damage with force damage) — a massive parasitic predator that hunts by detecting psychic signatures; it erupts from behind a bone ridge and attacks the party member with the highest Wisdom score; its crystalline hide refracts light, granting it advantage on saving throws against spells that deal radiant damage

Astral flotsam — a destroyed githyanki scout ship drifts near the corpse's shoulder, its three-person crew dead from exposure to concentrated divine energy; DC 14 Investigation reveals the ship's log, written in Gith, detailing the crew's mission to survey the corpse and their growing paranoia as the dreams began; the ship contains 2 potions of greater healing, a spell scroll of Dispel Magic, and a silver astral compass (non-magical, worth 150 gp)
secrets: The Great Wound — the killing blow that slew Auldrath — still radiates faint primordial energy; a DC 17 Arcana check at the wound's edge reveals that the energy signature matches no known primordial, supporting the theory that the killer's identity was deliberately erased from history; a character who touches the wound's edge must make a DC 16 Wisdom save or experience a flash of Auldrath's death — a moment of transcendent agony and a single image: a hand made of absolute nothingness reaching through a boundary that should have been impassable

The corpse is not rotating naturally — a DC 16 Investigation or Arcana check from the Approach reveals that the rotation follows a pattern, and that pattern corresponds to the orbits of the Inner Planes around the Material; Auldrath's body is still unconsciously maintaining boundaries even in death, and its rotation is a remnant of its divine function; this information becomes critical later when the party must time their extraction of the Confluence fragment to a specific rotational alignment

A small camp is visible on the corpse's left shoulder — this is Lithara Vex's base camp, marked by a single everburning torch and a ring of protective wards; DC 14 Perception to spot it from the Approach; approaching the camp triggers a Glyph of Warding (DC 15 Dexterity save or 5d8 thunder damage) unless the party calls out first; Lithara has been here for three years subjective time and is the foremost living expert on Auldrath's corpse

keyLocations.name: The Wound Gate
keyLocations.description: The primary entrance into Auldrath's interior is not the mouth or the nostrils or the ears — those are occupied by colonies of divine parasites so dense that penetrating them would require an army. Instead, explorers use the Wound Gate: a breach in the god's ribcage where the killing blow exited the back, punching through the divine flesh and bone to create an opening roughly sixty feet wide and two hundred feet tall. The edges of the wound have calcified into jagged formations of divine bone that look disturbingly like teeth, giving the entrance the appearance of a vast, vertical mouth frozen in a silent scream. The interior of the wound channel is coated with a thick layer of parasitic growth — bioluminescent organisms that have colonized the raw, exposed divine tissue like coral on a shipwreck. These organisms range from harmless (the glowing moss that provides dim amber light throughout the passage) to extremely dangerous (the Threshold Leeches — eyeless, eel-like creatures three to six feet long that are drawn to planar energy and will aggressively attack any creature carrying extraplanar items or bearing the mark of Threadwalker). The wound channel descends at a steep angle for approximately three hundred feet before opening into the thoracic cavity — a vast interior space the size of a small country, lit by the amber glow of crystallized ichor veins, where the calcified organs of a dead god loom like geological formations. The ribcage arches overhead like the vaults of an impossible cathedral, each rib a mile-long curve of divine bone two hundred feet thick. Between the ribs, the petrified intercostal muscles have partially dissolved, creating windows into the Astral Sea that let silver light stream through in shafts the size of city blocks. The Wound Gate is also where the party is most likely to encounter the Bone Warden for the first time — a construct of divine bone that patrols the wound channel on an ancient and unwavering route, executing the last command its dead master ever gave: guard the boundaries.
features: Wound Channel (60 ft wide, 200 ft tall, 300 ft descent) — the walls are coated with bioluminescent parasitic growth; the descent angle is approximately 45 degrees; DC 12 Athletics to descend safely with rope, DC 16 without; a fall from the midpoint deals 10d6 bludgeoning damage; the parasitic coating makes the walls slippery (DC 14 to maintain a grip while climbing)

Threshold Leeches (parasitic colony) — eyeless eel-like creatures 3-6 ft long that infest the wound channel in clusters of 4-8; they are dormant until they detect planar energy (extraplanar items, Threadwalker resonance, active spells from conjuration or abjuration schools); when triggered, they drop from the walls and ceiling; use stirge stats but replace blood drain with energy drain: attach on hit (DC 13 to detach), drain 1d4 force damage per round and suppress one random magic item on the target until removed; a DC 15 Nature check identifies them and reveals they can be repelled by bright light (Daylight spell or equivalent drives them into hiding for 1 hour)

Bone Warden Patrol Route — the Bone Warden passes through the wound channel every 30 minutes in a predictable circuit; DC 14 Perception to hear its approach (a rhythmic grinding of bone on bone that vibrates through the walls); the Warden fills most of the channel's width and attacks anything it does not recognize as belonging to Auldrath's corpse; a DC 18 Stealth check (group) to hide in side cavities as it passes, or it can be spoken to (see roleplay notes)

Parasitic Bioluminescence — the glowing organisms on the walls provide dim amber light throughout the wound channel; they react to vibration by briefly intensifying (any loud noise or impact causes a 5-second flare of bright light in a 30-ft radius); this can be used tactically to blind Threshold Leeches or signal allies, but also reveals the party's position to the Bone Warden

Thoracic Vista — at the bottom of the wound channel, the passage opens into the thoracic cavity; the first sight of the interior is overwhelming: a space so vast that the far wall is lost in amber haze, with cathedral-ribcage arches overhead and the calcified organs of a dead god rising from the cavity floor like mountains; DC 12 Wisdom save on first sight or be stunned for 1 round by the sheer cosmic scale
encounters: Threshold Leech Swarm — as the party descends the wound channel, a cluster of 6 Threshold Leeches (use stirge stats, CR 1/2 each, HP 2, AC 14, but with energy drain instead of blood drain: 1d4 force damage per round, suppresses one random magic item until detached) drops from the ceiling, targeting characters carrying the most magic items or bearing Threadwalker resonance; a 7th leech, larger than the rest (use stirge stats with HP 10 and 1d6 force drain), hangs back and drops only if the party seems weakened; tactics: they aim to drain and detach rather than kill, retreating into wall crevices when reduced to half their number

The Bone Warden (first encounter) — the construct rounds a bend in the wound channel, filling the passage with its bulk: a vaguely humanoid figure twelve feet tall, assembled from fragments of divine bone held together by amber light, with empty eye sockets that burn with a cold, purposeful glow; use shield guardian stats (CR 7, HP 142, AC 17) with the following modifications: immune to psychic and radiant damage, resistant to nonmagical physical damage, and it can cast Compelled Duel (DC 15) at will on a single target; it does not pursue beyond the wound channel; it can be reasoned with (see roleplay notes) but defaults to combat if not addressed in Celestial, Giant, or Primordial

A divine parasite hunting pack — 3 Marrow Stalkers (use phase spider stats, CR 3, HP 32, AC 13, but replace Ethereal Jaunt with the ability to phase through divine bone, emerging from walls and floors; poison damage becomes radiant damage) ambush the party near the bottom of the wound channel, using the bone walls to attack from unexpected angles; they are territorial predators and will retreat if 2 of 3 are killed
keyLocations.roleplayNotes: The Bone Warden is the first major NPC-like entity the party encounters inside the corpse. It is not intelligent in the conventional sense — it operates on the last command Auldrath gave it before dying: 'Guard the boundaries.' It interprets this literally and aggressively: anything that crosses a boundary (the wound is a boundary between inside and outside) is a target. However, it can be communicated with. It responds to speech in Celestial, Giant, or Primordial (Auldrath understood all three). A DC 16 Persuasion check in one of these languages can convince it that the party is here to restore boundaries (which is technically true — they are here to remove a Confluence fragment that is dissolving boundaries). On success, the Bone Warden steps aside and does not attack; on a critical success (natural 20 or total 25+), it provides a limited escort through the thoracic cavity, driving off parasites with its mere presence. On failure, it attacks. The Bone Warden cannot be permanently destroyed inside the corpse — if reduced to 0 HP, it collapses into a pile of bone fragments that reassemble over 1d4 hours. It can be avoided by timing its patrol route or hiding in side cavities. Lithara Vex, if the party has met her, knows the Bone Warden's patrol schedule and can advise them on how to avoid or communicate with it. She has a phrase in Celestial that puts it in standby mode for 10 minutes: 'The threshold holds. Rest, Warden.' She will share this reluctantly, as she considers the Warden a guardian of her research site.
secrets: The wound channel walls contain crystallized memory fragments — thin veins of amber crystal that, when touched with bare skin, produce brief flashes of Auldrath's memories; DC 14 Investigation to find a significant vein; DC 13 Wisdom save to maintain composure during the vision; the visions show: (1) Auldrath drawing the boundary between the Material Plane and the Shadowfell, a process that took centuries and required the god to exist in both planes simultaneously; (2) A divine council where Auldrath argued against the separation of the planes, warning that boundaries imposed from outside would eventually fail; (3) The moment of Auldrath's death — a hand of absolute nothingness reaching through a boundary and pulling the god apart; this last vision deals 2d6 psychic damage but also reveals that the killing blow came from INSIDE a boundary, suggesting the killer was something that existed between planes

A hidden side passage, concealed behind parasitic growth (DC 17 Investigation or DC 15 Perception for characters with darkvision), leads to a small chamber containing the remains of a previous expedition: three desiccated corpses in Astral Warden robes, dead for at least a century, their journals describing an earlier attempt to survey the corpse that was abandoned when the team leader began hearing the Dreaming Voice and refused to leave; the journals contain a partial map of the thoracic cavity and Marrow Halls, granting advantage on navigation checks in those areas; one corpse wears an Amulet of Proof Against Detection and Location (requires attunement)

The Bone Warden's patrol has changed — Lithara notices (if present) or a DC 18 Perception check reveals that the Warden has added new sections to its patrol route since the Confluence fragment activated, as if the fragment's boundary-dissolving energy has expanded the Warden's definition of what needs guarding; this is an early clue that the fragment is affecting even the corpse's residual divine systems

keyLocations.name: The Marrow Halls
keyLocations.description: The Marrow Halls are a labyrinthine network of tunnels that wind through the interior of Auldrath's divine bones — the colossal skeletal structure that gives the corpse its shape. The bones of a dead god are not like mortal bones. They are layered structures of incredible density, shot through with channels where divine marrow once flowed. That marrow has crystallized over the eons into a substance the color of dark honey, and it is in these crystallized marrow channels that the memories live. Auldrath's memories did not die with the god. They calcified, like everything else, and now they line the walls of the Marrow Halls in veins and deposits of amber crystal that play back moments of divine existence when disturbed. Walking through the Marrow Halls is like walking through a museum where the exhibits can reach out and grab you. Turn a corner and you might find yourself standing in a crystallized memory of the Dawn War — divine armies clashing across a sky that doesn't exist anymore, with weapons that rewrote the laws of physics. Or you might enter a pocket of profound stillness where a younger Auldrath sits alone at the boundary between two newborn planes, watching the first mortal soul cross from life to death, and feeling something that might be wonder or might be grief. The memories are not sequential or organized. They have been shaken loose by the Confluence fragment's activation and now play at random, overlapping and contradicting each other, creating a kaleidoscope of divine experience that is beautiful and deeply disorienting. Some memories are powerful enough to manifest physically — crystallized moments given form and substance by residual divinity. These Memory Golems are not hostile by nature, but they are fragments of divine consciousness running on autopilot, and they will defend themselves if threatened or if a character disrupts the memory they embody. The Marrow Halls are also the primary habitat of the corpse's internal ecosystem: creatures that have evolved in the marrow channels, feeding on crystallized memory and divine residue, creating a food chain that starts with microscopic memory-mites and ends with predators that hunt by psychic scent. Navigation is the primary challenge. The Halls branch and reconnect in three dimensions, with gravity varying by section (sometimes pulling toward the bone's center, sometimes toward its surface, sometimes in directions that don't correspond to any external reference). Without a guide or map, the party can wander for days. The partial map from the dead Astral Wardens helps, and Lithara Vex knows the routes intimately if she accompanies the party.
features: Crystallized Memory Veins — amber crystal deposits line the walls in branching patterns; touching a vein triggers a memory playback visible to everyone within 30 ft; DC 12 Wisdom save to maintain awareness that the memory is not real; failure means the character is absorbed into the memory for 1d4 rounds (incapacitated, experiencing the memory as if they were Auldrath); memories are random: roll 1d6: (1) Drawing boundaries between planes — serene, grants 1d4 temporary HP from divine calm; (2) Dawn War battle — violent, deals 1d6 psychic damage from sensory overload; (3) Argument with another god — tense, grants advantage on next Insight check; (4) Moment of divine loneliness — melancholy, DC 14 Wisdom save or gain the frightened condition for 1 minute from existential dread; (5) First mortal death witnessed — profound, grants resistance to necrotic damage for 1 hour; (6) The killing blow — traumatic, deals 2d6 psychic damage but reveals a clue about the fragment's location

Variable Gravity — gravity shifts between bone sections; DC 13 Acrobatics to adapt when gravity changes; failure means the character falls or floats uncontrollably for 1 round; the transition zones are marked by a faint amber shimmer visible with DC 12 Perception; characters who fail the Acrobatics check by 5 or more tumble into a different tunnel branch and must be found (DC 14 Survival or following the sound of their voice)

Marrow Channel Navigation — the tunnels form a three-dimensional maze; without a map or guide, navigation requires DC 16 Survival checks every 30 minutes of travel; failure means the party is lost and must spend 1d4 additional hours finding their bearings; the dead Wardens' partial map reduces this to DC 12; Lithara's guidance eliminates the need for checks in areas she has mapped (approximately 60% of the Halls); the silver compass provides general direction toward the skull but cannot account for the maze's complexity

Memory Resonance Zones — areas where multiple memory veins converge, creating overlapping visions that fill entire chambers; these zones are disorienting (disadvantage on Perception checks within them) but also rich with information; DC 15 Arcana to deliberately query a resonance zone for specific information about the corpse's layout, the fragment's nature, or Auldrath's history; success yields a truthful but cryptic answer delivered as a montage of memory fragments

Bioluminescent Ecosystem — the Marrow Halls support a complete food chain of divine parasites; most are harmless (glowing mites, crystal worms, luminescent fungi that grow on memory veins) but serve as an early warning system: when predators approach, the smaller organisms go dark, creating patches of sudden darkness that alert observant characters (DC 13 Perception) to incoming threats
encounters: Memory Golem — a crystallized moment of Auldrath's life given physical form: a twelve-foot humanoid figure made of amber crystal, replaying a fragment of the Dawn War in an endless loop; use stone golem stats (CR 10, HP 178, AC 17) with the following modifications: immune to psychic damage, vulnerable to thunder damage (which shatters crystal), and its slam attacks deal an additional 2d6 psychic damage as the target experiences a flash of the embedded memory; the golem is not inherently hostile — it ignores creatures that do not interfere with its memory loop; however, if the party needs to pass through the chamber it occupies, any physical contact with the golem or disruption of its memory loop (loud noise, bright light, dispel magic) triggers combat; it can be calmed with a DC 18 Arcana check to gently redirect the memory loop around the party, or a DC 16 Performance check to harmonize with the memory's emotional tone

Marrow Stalker Pack — 4 Marrow Stalkers (use phase spider stats, CR 3, HP 32, AC 13, radiant damage instead of poison, phase through bone instead of Ethereal Jaunt) ambush the party at a gravity transition zone where the disorientation makes the party vulnerable; they coordinate attacks, with 2 emerging from walls on each side of the tunnel; they target isolated characters and retreat into bone if they take more than 15 damage in a single round; a DC 15 Nature check mid-combat reveals that they fear Memory Golems and will flee if one is activated nearby

The Dreaming Voice (first manifestation) — as the party passes through a resonance zone, the overlapping memories suddenly coalesce into a single vision: a face of divine proportions, androgynous and beautiful and confused, materializing in the amber crystal of the walls; it speaks in a voice that is felt rather than heard, vibrating in the bones: 'You are... in me? I am... what am I? The boundaries... I was holding them... who let go?' The voice asks questions but does not wait for answers, cycling through confusion, recognition, and something like grief before dissolving back into scattered memories; this is not a combat encounter but a roleplay opportunity: characters who respond compassionately (DC 13 Persuasion or DC 14 Religion to frame the response in terms the divine subconscious would understand) receive a fragment of navigational intuition — advantage on Survival checks in the Marrow Halls for the next 8 hours; characters who respond with hostility or attempt to dominate the voice (DC 18 Intimidation) cause the surrounding memories to turn hostile, triggering a Memory Golem encounter
keyLocations.roleplayNotes: The Marrow Halls are where the scenario's tone shifts from exploration to psychological horror. The memories are not gentle — they are fragments of a divine mind that spanned eons and witnessed the creation and destruction of worlds. Characters who engage with the memories are exposing themselves to experiences that mortal minds were not designed to contain. Play up the dissonance between the intimate, personal nature of the memories (Auldrath's loneliness, Auldrath's wonder at the first sunset, Auldrath's grief at being forever excluded from the communities it protected) and the cosmic scale of the being who experienced them. The Dreaming Voice encounters should be eerie and sad rather than threatening — Auldrath is not trying to harm the party; it is a dying god's subconscious trying to remember what it was. The crystallized memories can serve as exposition delivery for players who want to understand the lore, or as atmospheric background for players who want to focus on dungeon-crawling. Lithara Vex is invaluable here — she has catalogued hundreds of memory veins and can guide the party to specific memories that provide useful information. She is also the only person who can explain why some memories manifest as golems (they are moments of intense divine emotion that crystallized with enough energy to achieve a crude form of autonomy). If Lithara is not present, the dead Wardens' journals provide basic but less detailed versions of this information.
secrets: One memory vein, hidden behind a particularly dense colony of crystal worms (DC 16 Investigation to find, DC 14 Nature to safely disperse the worms), contains Auldrath's memory of CREATING boundaries for the first time — the moment when the primordial chaos was divided into distinct planes; this memory is unique because it shows the process from the inside: Auldrath reaching into the undifferentiated everything and PULLING it apart, and the everything SCREAMING as it was separated; a character who experiences this memory must make a DC 16 Wisdom save or gain a permanent scar of insight: they understand intuitively that the Confluence is the everything trying to reassemble, and that it is not evil — it is in pain; this grants advantage on all checks to communicate with or understand the Confluence for the remainder of the campaign, but also imposes disadvantage on the final check to destroy a Confluence fragment (the character hesitates)

The Marrow Halls contain a hidden chamber that does not appear on any map — a pocket of preserved divine marrow that has not crystallized; it exists as a thick, warm, golden liquid that fills a spherical chamber 20 feet in diameter, accessible only through a narrow crack in the bone (DC 15 Acrobatics to squeeze through, Medium creatures only); the liquid marrow is the most concentrated source of divine energy in the corpse; a character who immerses themselves in it must make a DC 18 Constitution save: on success, they gain the benefits of a long rest and their maximum HP increases by 10 for 24 hours; on failure, they take 4d8 radiant damage as the divine energy overwhelms them; either way, the immersion triggers a vision of the Confluence fragment's exact location in the Skull Sanctum and the defenses surrounding it; the marrow can be bottled (up to 3 vials) and functions as a potion of superior healing (8d4+8 HP restored) with a side effect of 1d4 hours of divine visions (incapacitating for 1d4 rounds when consumed, then granting truesight for the remaining duration)

A specific sequence of memory veins, if activated in the correct order (DC 17 Investigation to determine the sequence from context clues in the memories, or Lithara can provide it if asked the right questions), tells the complete story of Auldrath's murder — not the sanitized version from historical texts but the truth: Auldrath was killed by an aspect of the Confluence itself, a fragment of the pre-creation intelligence that had been trapped inside one of the boundaries Auldrath maintained; the boundary between the Astral Sea and the Far Realm contained something that should not have been contained, and that something reached through its prison and unmade its jailer; this revelation recontextualizes the Confluence fragment in the skull — it may not be a random fragment that drifted here but the ORIGINAL piece, the one that killed Auldrath, returning to the scene of its crime

The gravity variations in the Marrow Halls follow a pattern that corresponds to the dead god's dream-state — when the dreams are calm, gravity is stable; when the dreams are agitated, gravity becomes chaotic; a DC 15 Arcana check to map the pattern reveals that the dream-state cycles every 2 hours between calm (45 minutes), restless (30 minutes), agitated (30 minutes), and nightmare (15 minutes); timing exploration to the calm phases makes navigation significantly easier (DC 12 Survival instead of DC 16), while the nightmare phase is extremely dangerous (gravity reverses completely every 1d4 rounds, DC 16 Acrobatics or Dexterity save to avoid taking 2d6 bludgeoning damage from being flung into walls)

keyLocations.name: The Heart Chamber
keyLocations.description: At the center of the thoracic cavity, suspended by calcified arteries the size of suspension bridge cables, hangs the Heart of Auldrath — a calcified organ the size of a fortress, roughly spherical, its surface covered in crystallized veins that pulse with that familiar amber glow. But the Heart is not entirely dead. It beats. Once every thirty seconds, the massive organ contracts with a deep, subsonic thud that vibrates through the entire corpse, and for a moment the amber glow intensifies to a blinding radiance before fading back. Each beat sends a pulse of residual divine energy through the corpse's crystallized circulatory system, and it is this energy that sustains the Dream — the dead god's unconscious mind, running on the fumes of a heart that refuses to stop. The Heart Chamber is the space surrounding the organ: a vast cavern within the thoracic cavity, roughly a mile in diameter, where the calcified lungs and other organs create a landscape of titanic biological architecture. The floor of the chamber is covered in a thick layer of divine sediment — crystallized divine fluids that have settled over millennia — and this sediment supports the corpse's most complex ecosystem. Creatures of extraordinary variety inhabit this space, from grazing herbivores that feed on divine crystal to predators of terrifying power that have evolved in the presence of concentrated divinity. The Heart itself is surrounded by the largest and most dangerous of these creatures: the Hearthbound, a colony of entities that have physically attached themselves to the Heart's surface and feed directly on each beat's pulse of energy. They are fiercely territorial and will attack anything that approaches the Heart. The party must pass through or around the Heart Chamber to reach the Skull Sanctum — the most direct route runs along the calcified aorta, a tunnel of divine tissue that leads from the Heart directly up into the head. But the aorta is the most heavily defended passage in the corpse, and the Hearthbound will not allow anything to enter it without a fight. Alternative routes exist through the Marrow Halls, but they add hours of travel through increasingly unstable dream-zones. The Heart Chamber is also where Lithara Vex has established her primary research station — a fortified camp in the shadow of a calcified lung, protected by wards and positioned to observe the Heart's beats. She has been studying the Heart for years and believes it holds the key to understanding how the Confluence fragment is interacting with Auldrath's residual divinity.
features: The Heartbeat — every 30 seconds, the Heart contracts and sends a pulse of divine energy through the corpse; within the Heart Chamber, each beat produces: (1) a shockwave of force (DC 12 Strength save or be pushed 10 feet away from the Heart), (2) a flash of bright amber light (creatures with sunlight sensitivity are blinded for 1 round), and (3) a momentary intensification of the Dream (DC 13 Wisdom save or experience a 6-second flash of Auldrath's memories, incapacitating the character for 1 round); characters can brace for the heartbeat if they know it's coming (no save required for the shockwave if braced, advantage on the Wisdom save)

Divine Sediment Floor — the chamber floor is covered in 1-3 feet of crystallized divine fluids; it is difficult terrain throughout; DC 14 Perception to spot sinkholes where the sediment conceals deeper cavities (falling in deals 1d6 bludgeoning and requires DC 13 Athletics to climb out); the sediment glows faintly and reacts to magic: any spell cast while standing on the sediment has its visual effects amplified dramatically (cosmetic but potentially useful for intimidation or signaling, granting advantage on Intimidation checks made with magic)

Calcified Organ Landscape — the lungs, liver, and other organs create a terrain of titanic biological structures; the calcified left lung is 800 feet tall and honeycombed with air passages that provide shelter and navigable tunnels; DC 12 Athletics to climb the lung's exterior; the liver is a solid mass of dark amber crystal, smooth-surfaced and slippery (DC 15 Acrobatics to traverse); between the organs, gaps of 100-500 feet create open killing fields where flying predators hunt

The Aorta — the main passage from Heart to skull, a tunnel of calcified arterial wall 50 feet in diameter; the interior is smooth and steep (ascending at 60 degrees for approximately 2 miles); DC 14 Athletics to ascend with climbing gear, DC 18 without; the walls are covered in Hearthbound organisms that attack anything entering the tunnel; the Aorta is the fastest route to the Skull Sanctum (2-3 hours of climbing) but the most dangerous

Lithara's Research Station — a fortified camp in a hollow carved into the calcified left lung, 200 feet above the chamber floor; protected by Alarm, Glyph of Warding (5d8 thunder, DC 15 Dex save), and Arcane Lock on the entrance; inside: a library of research notes, specimen jars containing preserved parasites, detailed maps of the Heart Chamber and Aorta, a scrying focus trained on the Heart, and Lithara's personal effects; the camp has supplies for approximately 3 months of solo habitation
encounters: Hearthbound Swarm — as the party approaches the Heart or attempts to enter the Aorta, 2 Hearthbound Drones (use gargoyle stats, CR 2, HP 52, AC 15, but replace all damage with radiant and add: when a drone is killed, it releases a pulse of stored divine energy in a 15-ft radius, dealing 2d6 radiant damage, DC 13 Dex save for half) and 1 Hearthbound Alpha (use manticore stats, CR 3, HP 68, AC 14, tail spikes become radiant energy bolts at range 100/200 ft, 1d8+3 radiant damage each, and it has an aura: all allies within 30 ft regenerate 5 HP at the start of each of their turns while within 60 ft of the Heart) attack; the Alpha directs the Drones to flank and drives the party away from the Aorta; if the Alpha is killed, the Drones become confused and flee; more Hearthbound arrive after 10 rounds (2 additional Drones per round) — this is meant to be an encounter the party must solve quickly or cleverly, not a war of attrition

Cerebral Devourer — this is the scenario's primary predator: a massive psychic entity that has migrated from the Skull Sanctum to hunt in the energy-rich Heart Chamber; use an intellect devourer stats scaled to CR 10 (HP 130, AC 16, Int 19, Wis 17, Cha 18) with the following abilities: (1) Psychic Crush (recharge 5-6): 60-ft cone, 6d8 psychic damage, DC 16 Intelligence save for half, and stunned for 1 round on failure; (2) Devour Thoughts: melee attack, +8 to hit, 3d8+4 psychic damage, and the target must succeed on a DC 16 Intelligence save or have one random proficiency suppressed for 1 hour; (3) Body Thief (as intellect devourer but DC 16); (4) Psychic Invisibility: the Devourer is invisible to any creature with an Intelligence score below 12 — it appears as a shimmer in the air that can be detected with DC 16 Perception; its true form is a pulsating mass of neural tissue the size of a horse, trailing tendrils of psychic energy, with a single enormous eye; it lurks in the divine sediment near the Heart, attracted by the party's concentrated thoughts; tactics: it targets the smartest party member first with Psychic Crush, then attempts Body Thief on an incapacitated target; it retreats into the sediment if reduced below 40 HP, burrowing away to heal and return in the Skull Sanctum for a second encounter

The Dreaming Voice (second manifestation) — during combat in the Heart Chamber, or during a quiet moment near the Heart, the amber glow intensifies and the Dreaming Voice speaks again, this time with more coherence: 'My heart still beats. I can feel you inside me. You are looking for the thing in my head — the splinter, the wrongness. It whispers to me. It tells me that I am still needed, that the boundaries I held are falling. Is that true? Are the boundaries falling?' This is a critical roleplay moment: the party can share information with the Dreaming Voice (DC 14 Persuasion to communicate clearly enough for the divine subconscious to understand), which may earn its cooperation in the Skull Sanctum; lying to the Voice (DC 18 Deception, contested by the Voice's passive Insight of 20) angers it, causing the Heartbeat to intensify (DC 15 saves instead of DC 12/13 for the next hour); telling it the truth — that yes, the boundaries are falling and the Confluence is reassembling — produces a long silence and then: 'Then I must wake up. But if I wake up, the dream ends, and everything inside me dies. Including you.'
keyLocations.roleplayNotes: The Heart Chamber is the scenario's emotional core. The Dreaming Voice's second manifestation should be played with increasing lucidity and pathos — Auldrath is waking up, slowly, drawn toward consciousness by the Confluence fragment's activity in its brain, and it is terrified of what waking up means. The god of boundaries is trapped on the threshold between life and death, and the irony is not lost on it. Lithara Vex's reaction to the Voice depends on her relationship with the party: if they have been respectful of her research and the corpse, she is moved to tears and urges the party to find a way to help Auldrath; if they have been destructive or dismissive, she is furious that they are disturbing her subject and may refuse to help further. The Heart Chamber is also where the party must make a key strategic decision: take the Aorta (fast but extremely dangerous, fighting through Hearthbound) or continue through the Marrow Halls (slower but allows them to avoid the worst of the Heart's defenses). Lithara advocates for the Marrow Halls route, having never dared the Aorta herself. She can provide a detailed map of a Marrow Hall route to the skull that takes approximately 8 hours but avoids major combat. The Bone Warden does not enter the Heart Chamber — it patrols the bone structure, not the soft tissue — so the party cannot rely on it for protection here.
secrets: The Heart is not beating on its own — a DC 18 Arcana check or DC 16 Medicine check (with proficiency) reveals that the Confluence fragment in the skull is stimulating the Heart through the crystallized nervous system; the fragment NEEDS the Heart to beat to power its amplification of boundary-dissolution; if the Heart could be stopped, the fragment would lose its divine amplification and be much easier to extract; however, stopping the Heart would also kill every organism in the corpse (including the party if they don't leave quickly), end the Dream permanently, and eliminate any possibility of Auldrath ever being restored — a moral dilemma with no clean answer

Lithara's research notes (found at her station or shared if she trusts the party) reveal that the Heartbeat has been accelerating — when she first arrived three years ago, it beat once every two minutes; now it beats every thirty seconds; she has calculated that at the current rate of acceleration, the Heart will reach a continuous beat — effectively restarting Auldrath's circulatory system — in approximately six days; she does not know what will happen then, but her best guess is catastrophic: a dead god's body restarting without a living soul to control it would release enough divine energy to create a new convergence zone the size of a continent

Hidden in the divine sediment near the Heart's base (DC 17 Investigation, or the Cerebral Devourer's lair can be tracked here after it flees) is a cache of items from previous explorers: a +1 mace with the property that it deals an extra 1d6 radiant damage against undead and constructs (useful against Memory Golems and the Bone Warden), a Cloak of Protection, 3 potions of greater healing, a sealed journal belonging to a Convergence Herald (an agent of the Confluence) that details the Herald's mission to protect the fragment and accelerate the Heart — proof that the fragment's placement here is deliberate, not accidental

The Heart contains a resonance frequency that, if matched with magical vibration (DC 17 Performance check with a musical instrument, or a carefully modulated Thaumaturgy or Prestidigitation), can temporarily synchronize the party's heartbeats with Auldrath's — for 1 hour after synchronization, all party members are immune to the Heartbeat's shockwave and Wisdom save effects, have advantage on saves against dream effects in the Skull Sanctum, and can perceive the Dreaming Voice's communications clearly without skill checks; the frequency can be determined by studying Lithara's research (DC 14 Investigation) or by asking the Dreaming Voice directly

keyLocations.name: The Skull Sanctum
keyLocations.description: The interior of Auldrath's skull is where reality ends and the Dream begins. The skull itself is a dome of divine bone three miles in diameter, smooth on the interior surface, and every inch of it is covered in active memory veins — not the scattered fragments found in the Marrow Halls but a continuous, interconnected web of crystallized memory that constitutes the dead god's brain. It is all firing. All of it, simultaneously, playing back every moment of Auldrath's existence in an overlapping cacophony of divine experience that should be incomprehensible but isn't, because the Confluence fragment at the center of the skull is organizing it. The fragment floats in the exact center of the skull cavity: a shard of crystallized pre-creation intelligence the size of a human fist, pulsing with a light that is not amber but prismatic — every color at once, shifting and merging, the visual signature of undifferentiated reality. It is embedded in a mass of neural crystal — Auldrath's calcified brain tissue — and tendrils of its prismatic light extend outward into the memory web like roots, drawing on Auldrath's residual divinity to amplify its boundary-dissolving signal across the Astral Sea. The air in the Skull Sanctum is not air. It is Dream — a medium of manifested thought that fills the skull cavity like water fills a bowl. Breathing it is possible but disorienting: every inhalation carries fragments of Auldrath's dreams, and every exhalation releases fragments of your own thoughts into the medium, where they can manifest visibly. The Dream is thick with manifestations: figures from Auldrath's memories walk the curved interior surface of the skull as if it were flat ground, enacting scenes from the god's life in an endless loop. Some are harmless ghosts. Others are Memory Golems — moments of intense emotion crystallized into physical form by the fragment's amplifying effect. And some are Dream Manifestations: things that Auldrath is dreaming NOW, shaped by the fragment's influence, that are neither memory nor imagination but something more dangerous — reality being rewritten by a sleeping god's subconscious desires. The gravity in the skull is entirely dream-logic: characters can walk on any surface — floor, walls, ceiling — and 'down' is wherever they believe it to be, requiring a DC 13 Wisdom check to maintain a consistent orientation. The fragment cannot simply be grabbed and removed. It is integrated into the neural crystal, and extracting it requires a delicate process of severing its connections to the memory web without triggering a catastrophic feedback loop. If the extraction is botched, the Dream collapses into the fragment, creating a reality implosion that would destroy the corpse and everything within a hundred miles. The party must navigate the Skull Sanctum, survive its defenses, and perform the extraction — all while the Dream grows increasingly aware of their presence and increasingly hostile to their purpose.
features: Dream Medium Atmosphere — the skull cavity is filled with manifested thought instead of air; breathing is possible but each inhalation requires a DC 12 Wisdom save or the character experiences a 6-second flash of Auldrath's current dream (incapacitated for 1 round); the Dream medium is also a visual phenomenon: thoughts and emotions manifest as visible colors and shapes around characters' heads, making Stealth checks in the Skull Sanctum made at disadvantage (your intentions are literally visible) unless the character succeeds on a DC 15 Deception check to mask their thoughts; conversely, the medium allows telepathic communication between all characters within the skull without the need for spells or abilities

Dream-Logic Gravity — characters can walk on any surface within the skull; 'down' is determined by belief; DC 13 Wisdom check to establish personal gravity (failure means the character floats uncontrollably for 1d4 rounds or until they calm themselves with a DC 10 Wisdom check as a bonus action); characters who have synchronized their heartbeats with the Heart make this check with advantage; gravity can be weaponized: a DC 16 Arcana check allows a character to impose their gravity on another willing creature within 30 ft, or a DC 18 check on an unwilling creature (Wisdom save to resist)

Memory Web — the interconnected neural crystal covering the skull's interior; it glows with continuous playback of Auldrath's memories; touching the web directly triggers a full immersion experience: DC 16 Wisdom save or be absorbed into the memory web for 1d6 rounds (incapacitated, experiencing Auldrath's life from the inside); the web can be navigated intentionally with a DC 18 Arcana check, allowing a character to search Auldrath's memories for specific information (treat as Legend Lore with no material component, but the casting time is the 1d6 rounds of immersion)

The Confluence Fragment — visible at the skull's center as a fist-sized shard of prismatic crystal embedded in neural tissue; it radiates anti-boundary energy in a 60-ft radius: within this radius, all extradimensional spaces (bags of holding, portable holes, etc.) malfunction (50% chance per round of dumping contents into the Dream medium), teleportation fails automatically, and the boundaries between creatures blur (each round, each character in the radius must make a DC 14 Charisma save or briefly merge perceptions with a random other character in the radius, sharing thoughts and senses for 6 seconds — disorienting but not damaging); the fragment pulses in sync with the Heartbeat, and its anti-boundary effect intensifies during each pulse

Dream Manifestation Spawning — the Skull Sanctum continuously generates Dream Manifestations: creatures shaped by Auldrath's subconscious; every 10 minutes (or every 3 rounds during combat), a new manifestation appears: roll 1d4: (1) A peaceful memory-figure that wanders harmlessly; (2) A confused figure that approaches the party and tries to interact, dissolving if touched; (3) A hostile manifestation — Auldrath's nightmare of its own killer — that attacks the nearest creature (use wraith stats, CR 5, but dealing psychic damage instead of necrotic, and it dissolves after 3 rounds regardless of HP); (4) A defensive manifestation — the Dream recognizing the party as intruders and producing a guardian (use Memory Golem stats from Marrow Halls encounter)
encounters: The Skull Gauntlet — upon entering the Skull Sanctum, the Dream reacts to the party's presence with a wave of defensive manifestations: 2 Dream Wraiths (wraith stats, CR 5, HP 67, AC 13, psychic damage instead of necrotic, life drain becomes thought drain: target's Intelligence score is reduced by 1d4 on a failed DC 14 Constitution save, restored after a short rest; dissolve after 5 rounds) and 1 Memory Golem (stone golem stats, CR 10, HP 178, AC 17, additional 2d6 psychic damage on hits, vulnerable to thunder) emerge from the memory web and attack; the manifestations reform 1 hour after being destroyed unless the party has synchronized with the Heartbeat (which marks them as 'part of Auldrath' to the Dream's defenses, reducing encounters by half) or convinced the Dreaming Voice to grant them passage (which suppresses hostile manifestations entirely for 2 hours)

Cerebral Devourer (final encounter) — if the Devourer retreated from the Heart Chamber, it is here, fully healed and nesting in the neural crystal within 30 feet of the fragment, feeding on the amplified psychic energy; it has grown stronger from proximity to the fragment: HP 150 (up from 130), and it gains a new ability — Dream Anchor: as a bonus action, it can tether itself to the Dream medium, becoming immune to forced movement and gaining +2 AC until the start of its next turn; it fights to the death to protect its food source; if the Devourer was killed in the Heart Chamber, replace this encounter with a Convergence Echo — a reflection of the party from an alternate timeline where they failed, using the party's own stats and abilities but controlled by the DM, representing the Dream's attempt to process and counter the intruders by creating copies

The Extraction — the scenario's climax is not a combat encounter but a complex skill challenge that takes place while the Dream fights to prevent the fragment's removal; the extraction requires 5 successes before 3 failures using the following skills (each character can attempt one check per round, and a character cannot use the same skill twice in succession): Arcana DC 16 (severing a tendril of the fragment's connection to the memory web), Medicine DC 15 (stabilizing the neural crystal to prevent feedback), Religion DC 17 (invoking Auldrath's domain of boundaries to create a buffer between fragment and brain), Sleight of Hand DC 16 (physically manipulating the fragment without disturbing adjacent crystal), Performance DC 14 (maintaining the heartbeat synchronization to keep the Dream stable); EACH FAILURE triggers a consequence: 1st failure — a psychic shockwave deals 3d6 psychic damage to all characters within 30 ft of the fragment (DC 15 Intelligence save for half); 2nd failure — the Dream becomes hostile, spawning 2 Dream Wraiths that attack during the extraction; 3rd failure — catastrophic feedback: the fragment begins a chain reaction that will destroy the skull in 5 rounds, forcing the party to flee (they can attempt the extraction again after the reaction subsides, but the DCs increase by 2); SUCCESS (5 successes) — the fragment separates from the neural crystal with a sound like breaking glass, the memory web goes dark, the Dream shudders and stills, and the Dreaming Voice speaks one last time: 'The splinter is out. The boundaries I held... they need someone to hold them again. Will you hold them? Will someone?' The fragment is now a portable item — a fist-sized prismatic crystal that pulses with warmth and whispers at the edge of perception

Optional: The Dream Collapses (consequence of stopping the Heart or botching the extraction catastrophically) — if the party chose to stop the Heart or if the extraction chain reaction is not escaped in time, the Dream begins to die; the skull cavity fills with a rising tide of grey light as memories dissolve one by one; all creatures in the skull take 2d6 psychic damage per round (no save) as the Dream medium becomes toxic; the fragment ejects itself from the neural crystal (it wants to survive) and can be grabbed with a DC 12 Dexterity check as it tumbles through the dissolving Dream; the party has 10 rounds to exit the skull before it collapses entirely, dealing 10d6 bludgeoning damage to anyone inside; the Bone Warden, if it still functions, attempts to seal the skull's exits to prevent the collapse from spreading to the rest of the corpse, creating a final obstacle (DC 18 Athletics or Persuasion in Celestial to get past)
keyLocations.roleplayNotes: The Skull Sanctum is the climax of the scenario, and the tone should be overwhelming — the party is inside the literal mind of a dead god, and the mind is waking up. Every sensation is amplified: emotions are visible as colors, thoughts echo as whispers, and the boundary between self and other is dissolving. Characters should feel their individuality becoming porous — they catch glimpses of each other's thoughts, feel phantom emotions that belong to Auldrath, and struggle to remember which memories are theirs and which are the god's. The Dreaming Voice is at its most coherent here, and its final communication should be played as a dying wish — Auldrath knows it cannot wake up, knows the Dream is ending, and its last concern is not for itself but for the boundaries it was made to protect. The extraction skill challenge should be narrated with tension and consequence: each success should produce a dramatic visual (a tendril of prismatic light severing and recoiling, neural crystal cracking and darkening) and each failure should produce real fear (the skull shaking, the Dream screaming, the fragment pulsing faster). The party's decision about whether to take the fast or careful approach to extraction should feel meaningful — speed risks catastrophe, but delay means more Dream Manifestation encounters. If the Dreaming Voice has been befriended, it actively helps during the extraction, manifesting as a pair of divine hands that hold the neural crystal steady, granting advantage on Medicine and Sleight of Hand checks during the challenge. If the Voice has been antagonized or ignored, it actively opposes the extraction, imposing disadvantage on Religion checks and spawning additional hostile manifestations.
secrets: The fragment is alive — not sentient in the way a creature is sentient, but aware in the way a mathematical equation is aware of its own solution; when extracted, it does not go inert; it continues to pulse and whisper, and characters who hold it for more than an hour begin to hear it more clearly: it speaks of unity, of the beauty of a reality without borders, and of the loneliness of separation; a DC 18 Wisdom save each hour to avoid becoming sympathetic to its message; failure doesn't mean the character is dominated — it means they genuinely begin to question whether the separation of the planes was the right choice; this becomes a character-driven subplot that echoes through the remaining scenarios

The Dreaming Voice's final request — 'Will you hold the boundaries?' — is not metaphorical; if a character explicitly says yes, the dead god's last fragment of divine purpose passes to them in the form of a divine boon: Threshold Warden — once per long rest, the character can cast Banishment without expending a spell slot, and they have advantage on all saving throws against effects that would move them to another plane against their will; however, they also gain a permanent sense of every planar boundary within 1 mile, which manifests as a constant low hum in the back of their mind that intensifies near convergence zones (disadvantage on Perception checks that rely on hearing while within 100 feet of a convergence zone or planar portal)

If the extraction succeeds cleanly (5 successes, 0 failures), a hidden memory is unlocked — Auldrath's very last thought before death: a vision of ALL the Confluence fragments and their locations across the Astral Sea, including the fragment in the Planar Crucible and the one at the Spire of Echoes; this information is delivered as a flash of cartographic intuition that permanently marks the silver compass with the locations of all remaining fragments, eliminating the need for navigation checks to find them; this is an enormous reward for a perfect extraction and should be narrated with appropriate weight

The skull itself, once the fragment is removed, begins to change — the memory web dims and the Dream fades, but the bone structure remains, and without the fragment's destabilizing influence, the skull becomes the most stable boundary in the Astral Sea; Zerith-Ka, if contacted, recognizes its potential as a replacement for the failing Threshold Citadel — a new fortress for the Astral Wardens, built inside the skull of the god who protected boundaries; this decision has campaign-level consequences and should be presented to the party as a choice, not a foregone conclusion

synopsis: The silver compass points deeper into the Astral Sea, toward a darkness visible against the silver void — a shape that resolves, impossibly, into the petrified corpse of a dead god. Auldrath, the divine custodian of boundaries and thresholds, has drifted through the Astral for eons since its murder during the Dawn War. Now a Confluence fragment — a shard of the pre-creation intelligence that seeks to reunify all planes — has lodged itself in the dead god's skull like a splinter in a wound, and the residual divinity saturating the corpse is amplifying the fragment's power a thousandfold. The party must enter the continent-sized corpse, navigate divine bone caverns haunted by crystallized memories, survive the parasitic ecosystems that feed on dead divinity, and extract the fragment from the god's calcified brain — all while contending with the fact that Auldrath is still dreaming, and its dreams manifest as reality inside the corpse. The deeper the party ventures, the more powerful and unpredictable the dreams become, until in the Skull Sanctum itself, the boundary between dream and waking dissolves entirely. The extraction is not merely a physical challenge but a moral one: the Confluence fragment is the thing that killed Auldrath, returning to amplify its original crime, and removing it will end the dead god's dream forever. The party must decide how much they are willing to sacrifice to save a reality that was built on the suffering of the being whose body they are desecrating.
hook: The silver compass has been pulling northeast for three days — a steady, insistent tug that has grown warmer with each passing hour until the metal is almost too hot to hold. Zerith-Ka's voice echoes in your memory: 'The second fragment is lodged in something old. Something divine. You will know it when you see it, and you will wish you hadn't.' She was right. You see it now, emerging from the Astral haze like a continent surfacing from a silver sea: a body. A humanoid body forty miles long, curled in a posture of sleep or death, its features still recognizable despite being carved from stone that was once flesh. The face is peaceful. The eyes are closed. The hands are folded over a chest that has been split open by a wound that still glows faintly with primordial energy. It is the corpse of a god, and it is the largest thing you have ever seen, and as you draw closer, you feel something that is not the compass pulling you — a psychic tug, gentle and confused, as if something inside the corpse has noticed you and is trying to remember what living things are. The compass needle locks on the skull. The warmth becomes almost unbearable. And in the silence of the Astral Sea, you hear — or perhaps feel — the faintest echo of a heartbeat, coming from deep inside the corpse. Something is still alive in there. Or something is dreaming that it is.

acts.title: Act 1: The Threshold
acts.description: The party approaches the corpse of Auldrath, makes first contact with the exterior ecosystem and the planar archaeologist Lithara Vex, and gains entry to the corpse's interior through the Wound Gate. This act establishes the scenario's tone — cosmic wonder mixed with creeping unease — and introduces the key NPCs and threats. The party must navigate the divine haze, survive the Approach's predators, negotiate or fight past the Bone Warden, and descend into the thoracic cavity. By the act's end, they should have a basic understanding of the corpse's layout, the nature of the Confluence fragment, and the terrible truth that Auldrath is still dreaming.
objectives: Navigate the Approach and reach the corpse's surface safely
Locate and make contact with Lithara Vex at her shoulder camp
Gain entry through the Wound Gate (by stealth, combat, or negotiation with the Bone Warden)
Descend into the thoracic cavity and establish a base of operations
Learn the basic layout of the corpse's interior and plan a route to the skull

scenes.name: Into the Divine Haze
scenes.description: The party enters the region of Astral space within ten miles of Auldrath's corpse, where residual divine energy creates a golden mist filled with parasitic life forms. The divine haze is beautiful and dangerous — it produces euphoria, attracts psychic predators, and provides the party's first direct exposure to the unsettling reality that they are approaching something that was once a god.
scenes.readAloud: The silver void of the Astral Sea begins to change. A golden haze seeps into the emptiness like dawn breaking in a world without a sun, and the air — if you can call it air in a place where breathing is optional — takes on a taste like honey and lightning. Motes of amber light drift through the haze in lazy spirals, thousands of them, millions, each one a tiny organism feeding on energy that leaks from something enormous ahead. The compass is almost too hot to hold now. Its needle doesn't just point — it strains, pulling the instrument forward in your grip as if magnetized to something beyond your sight. And then the haze thins for a moment, a gap in the golden curtain, and you see it. A face. A face the size of a mountain range, carved from dark stone, eyes closed in an expression of absolute peace. It is beautiful in the way that a glacier is beautiful — vast and indifferent and capable of destroying you without noticing. The haze closes again, and the face is gone, but the image burns in your mind. You are approaching the corpse of a god. The motes of light drift closer, curious, and somewhere in the golden haze, something much larger than a mote begins to move.

skillChecks.success: The character filters the divine haze without ill effect and can breathe normally. They notice the euphoric quality of the air without succumbing to it.
skillChecks.failure: The character feels a wave of irrational euphoria — everything is beautiful, nothing can go wrong, the corpse of a dead god is the most wonderful thing they have ever seen. Disadvantage on Wisdom checks for 1 hour.

skillChecks.success: The character can actively filter the divine energy, converting the haze's euphoric effect into a protective barrier. They gain 1d8 temporary hit points as residual divinity reinforces their vitality.
skillChecks.failure: The character's attempt to manipulate the divine energy backfires, producing a brief flare of amber light visible for a mile in every direction. Any predators in the area are now aware of the party's position.

skillChecks.success: The character spots Lithara Vex's camp on the corpse's left shoulder — a tiny pinprick of light from an everburning torch, surrounded by a faint shimmer of protective wards. This gives the party a destination on the surface.
skillChecks.failure: The character does not notice the camp and will have to search for it after landing on the surface, requiring additional time and exposure to surface predators.

skillChecks.success: The character identifies a safe landing zone on the corpse's surface — a flat expanse of calcified skin near the left collarbone, free of major parasite colonies and with a clear line of sight to the shoulder.
skillChecks.failure: The party lands in a less favorable location — possibly on a section of unstable calcified flesh, near a parasite nest, or on an amber crystal lake that cracks under their weight.

enemies: 1 Void Grazer (bulette stats, CR 5, HP 94, AC 17, flying 40 ft, force damage instead of all damage types, advantage on saves against radiant spells)
combatEncounters.tactics: The Void Grazer detects the party's psychic signatures from within the haze and charges from below, targeting the character with the highest Wisdom score. It uses its leap ability to close distance rapidly, erupting from the golden mist without warning. If reduced to half HP, it attempts to swallow a Small creature or grab a Medium creature and carry it into the haze to feed in private. It flees if reduced below 20 HP.
combatEncounters.terrain: Open Astral space within the divine haze. The haze provides light obscurement beyond 60 ft. There is no ground — all combat is three-dimensional. Characters who are not flying must use Astral movement (Intelligence × 3 ft per round) or be carried. The Void Grazer can hide in the haze by going still (DC 16 Perception to spot it when motionless).

scenes.roleplayNotes: This scene sets the tone for the entire scenario. The approach to the corpse should be narrated with a mix of wonder and dread — the players should feel the sheer impossible scale of what they are approaching. The divine haze is not hostile but it is alien, and the parasitic organisms that inhabit it are a reminder that even a dead god's body is an ecosystem. If the party tries to communicate with the Luminous Motes or the Void Grazer, neither is intelligent enough to respond — they are animals, albeit animals that evolved in the presence of divinity. The compass's behavior should be emphasized: it is almost painfully hot, and its needle is locked on the skull with an urgency that suggests the fragment is actively calling to it.
loot: From the destroyed githyanki scout ship (if investigated): 2 potions of greater healing, a spell scroll of Dispel Magic (3rd level), a silver astral compass (non-magical, worth 150 gp), and the ship's log (written in Gith — can be translated with Comprehend Languages or a DC 16 Intelligence check by a character proficient in Linguistics or who speaks Gith)

scenes.name: Lithara's Camp
scenes.description: The party reaches the surface of Auldrath's corpse and locates the camp of Lithara Vex, a human wizard and planar archaeologist who has been studying the dead god for three subjective years. Lithara is brilliant, half-mad, and the best source of information the party will find about the corpse's interior, the Confluence fragment, and the nature of the Dream. This scene is primarily roleplay — gaining Lithara's trust, learning what she knows, and convincing her to help.
scenes.readAloud: The camp is smaller than you expected — a single tent of waxed canvas, a ring of glowing runes etched into the calcified skin of a dead god, and an everburning torch jammed into a crack in the divine flesh like a candle in a birthday cake. Around the tent, a semicircle of specimen jars catches the amber light: things float in preservation fluid that you do not want to examine too closely. Notes and diagrams are pinned to the tent's exterior with bone pins, fluttering in a breeze that shouldn't exist in the Astral Sea but does anyway, because the corpse makes its own weather. And standing at the edge of the warded circle, watching your approach with eyes that are simultaneously terrified and delighted, is a woman who looks like she hasn't slept in a year. Her hair is streaked with premature grey, her robes are covered in amber stains and mathematical equations written in chalk, and she is holding a wand in one hand and a half-eaten piece of dried meat in the other. 'Oh,' she says, and her voice cracks from disuse. 'Oh, you're REAL. I can tell because you're ugly. The dream-people are always beautiful.' She squints. 'Relatively ugly. No offense. Please don't be a hallucination. I have SO much to tell someone.'

skillChecks.success: Lithara relaxes and invites the party into her warded circle. She shares her research freely — maps, notes on the Dream cycle, information about the Bone Warden's patrol schedule, and her theory about the Confluence fragment's interaction with Auldrath's residual divinity.
skillChecks.failure: Lithara remains suspicious, sharing only basic information. She does not reveal her maps or the Bone Warden's standby phrase. She can be won over later with gifts (spell components, food from the Material Plane, or news from the outside world) or by demonstrating respect for her research.

skillChecks.success: The character impresses Lithara with their understanding of planar theory. She treats them as a colleague rather than an interruption and shares her most sensitive finding: the Heartbeat is accelerating, and she believes the corpse will catastrophically reactivate within six days.
skillChecks.failure: Lithara is politely dismissive of the character's arcane knowledge. 'That's very Material Plane of you,' she says. She still helps, but she explains things in condescending detail that wastes time.

skillChecks.success: The character realizes that Lithara is not just studying the corpse — she is emotionally attached to it. She has been listening to the Dreaming Voice for three years and has developed a protective, almost maternal attitude toward Auldrath's subconscious. She does not want the Dream to end and may resist or sabotage the extraction if she believes it will kill the Dream permanently.
skillChecks.failure: The character takes Lithara at face value — an eccentric scholar studying a fascinating phenomenon. They miss the emotional undercurrent and may be surprised by her reaction later.

skillChecks.success: The character notices signs of prolonged divine energy exposure: Lithara's pupils occasionally flash amber, her skin has a faint luminous quality in dim light, and her pulse rate is synchronized with the Heartbeat. She is slowly being absorbed into the corpse's ecosystem. She has approximately one year before the process becomes irreversible.
skillChecks.failure: The character notices that Lithara looks tired and malnourished but attributes it to the hardships of solo field research. They miss the signs of divine absorption.

scenes.roleplayNotes: Lithara Vex is the scenario's most complex NPC. She is genuinely brilliant — her three years of research have produced the most comprehensive study of a dead god's corpse ever attempted — but the isolation and divine exposure have eroded her grip on conventional reality. She talks too fast, jumps between topics, occasionally addresses remarks to people who aren't there (dream-figures she has been conversing with), and has a habit of absently touching the calcified flesh beneath her feet with the tenderness of someone stroking a sleeping animal. She is not evil or crazy — she is a scientist who has fallen in love with her subject and cannot bear the thought of it ending. She will help the party reach the fragment because she understands the threat the Convergence poses, but she will advocate for solutions that preserve the Dream: extracting the fragment without killing Auldrath's subconscious, finding a way to sustain the Heartbeat without the fragment's stimulation, or even allowing the god to wake up and resume its role as guardian of boundaries. Her Celestial standby phrase for the Bone Warden ('The threshold holds. Rest, Warden.') is something she will share only if she trusts the party — it represents her deepest intimacy with the corpse and she guards it jealously. She speaks Common, Celestial, Draconic, and Primordial. She is a 9th-level wizard (School of Divination) with a focus on detection and analysis spells rather than combat magic.
